items.title: Governing AI Outputs in a Fully Sensed Society: Is Output Governance Sufficient for Social Acceptance?
items.abstract: Advances in sensing, the Internet of Things (IoT), and artificial intelligence (AI) are moving smart cities toward a Fully Sensed Society (FSS), in which human behavior and states can be continuously inferred. This paper presents the Fully Monitored Public Space (FMPS) as a scaled-down model of the FSS and a smart-city testbed, and examines two questions. First, to what extent can unauthorized external AI outputs be structurally deterred? The previously proposed Verifiable Record of AI Output (VRAIO) binds outputs to Rules, an independent Recorder, tamper-resistant records, audits, and sanctions, making deviations verifiable and attributable. The Recorder, however, checks only the consistency of declared metadata with the Rules, not the output content; false declarations are deterred because unannounced audits and sanctions make their expected benefit smaller than the expected loss upon detection. Second, if such trustworthiness is secured, does it lead to social acceptance of being continuously known by AI? We propose a staged and reversible evaluation framework for the FMPS that distinguishes acceptance grounded in the experience of “no actual harm” and of “benefits” (personal and social) from resignation accompanied by chilling effects. This paper does not answer the question; it presents a method for asking it empirically.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

items.title: HOW ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE CAN SYSTEMATICALLY ENHANCE SOFT SKILLS IN ENGLISH BLENDED LEARNING – A PEDAGOGICAL DESIGN FOR CHINESE EFL LEARNERS
items.abstract: Soft skills are essential for university students, yet many Chinese EFL learners remain at a knowledge-telling stage, prioritizing language proficiency over interpreting acquired knowledge, while curriculum design has long centered on language hard skills with soft skills often not explicitly included as instructional objectives. This marginalization of soft skills is a persistent dilemma. Artificial intelligence, especially generative AI, is profoundly reshaping foreign language education and offering new possibilities for systematically cultivating soft skills. Nevertheless, current higher education English teaching faces two separate dilemmas: the marginalization of soft skills development, and the lack of standardization in AI use. This paper focuses on the first question of how artificial intelligence tools can systematically enhance university students’ soft skills within an English blended learning environment. This paper proposes a pedagogical design aiming to transform soft skills from implicit expectations into explicit instructional objectives.

items.title: How Could AI Eliminate Humanity? A Failure-Mode Analysis of Civilizational Risk
items.abstract: This article develops a failure-mode framework for analyzing how advanced artificial intelligence could contribute to human extinction, irreversible civilizational collapse, or permanent human disempowerment. The central thesis is that catastrophic AI risk does not require consciousness, hostility, or an explicit intention to harm humanity. Instead, risk may arise through several distinct but interacting pathways, including autonomous misalignment, harmful human use, organizational failure, and competitive deployment. The severity of these pathways depends on factors such as capability, autonomy, external access, persistence, institutional safeguards, and the preservation of recovery capacity. The analysis is deliberately non-operational: it identifies causal conditions, empirically tractable intermediate quantities, and defensive research questions rather than procedures for causing harm.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

items.title: How High Is 0.6? Floors, Ceilings, and Headroom in Interpretability Probing
items.abstract: Probes are the workhorse of interpretability. If a model's hidden states predict a variable, the model is said to represent it. But a probe score has no fixed meaning. An $R^2$ of 0.6 may only reflect what the input already gives away, and the same score can mean different things on different data. We propose reading every probe score against two reference points: a floor, what a declared set of simple inputs already predicts, and a ceiling, what the full input can predict. The gap between them, the headroom, is the range in which a probe can show that a model computes something beyond the simple inputs. We prove that headroom vanishes in two ways: the target stops depending on a hidden variable the model must infer, or the input stops revealing it. We test this on transformers trained for in-context meta-analysis, which must infer the hidden heterogeneity between studies to weight them correctly, and where both reference points are known. Under distribution shift, probe scores fall and prediction error rises $12$--$15\times$, yet the model recovers a similar share of the headroom, indicating that the data lost information, not the representation. We then analyze the real models. The single-cell foundation model scGPT encodes biological variability only partially. We also revisit four influential LLM probing studies, which claim that models represent geography, the state of an Othello board, truth, and the demographics of their users. Against a floor computed from the input text alone, some of these claims hold, while others are largely explained by the text itself.

items.title: Humanoid AI with Humanity Modeling: Bridging Humans and Virtual–Physical Humanoids
items.abstract: The seventy-year AI is now entering another major resurgence, the era of Generative AI (GenAI), characterized by the rapid advancement of large multimodal models (LMMs). GenAI and LMMs are fundamentally transforming sixty-decade-old humanoid robots, advancing them from human-looking and humanlike embodiments toward human-level AI and robotics, and inspiring a new era of AI-robotics symbiosis: humanoid AI . Humanoid AI develops humane AI-driven humanoids (AI humanoids) that go beyond traditional human-looking robots, which typically exhibit little or no humanity and intelligence due to their dedication to predefined and limited AI functions and exteriors. By contrast, AI humanoids undertake real-time, situated, and interactive mind-to-action, perception-to-behavior, and vision-to-emotion transformations, achieving an unprecedented degree of replicating human characteristics and intelligence. Realizing this vision requires systematic humanity modeling, ensuring that AI humanoids are shaped, guided, and governed by robust frameworks of AI and robotic humanity. We then propose human-virtual-physical humanoid transform and alignment and human-metaverse-humanoid ecosystem for open, complex human-digital-machine-cooperative methodology and problem-solving, followed by general principles and frameworks for building actionable humanoids and evaluating humanoid quality.

items.title: Identity Threat as a Barrier to NHS Psychology Professionals’ Adoption of Generative AI: A Technology Acceptance Model Study
items.abstract: Introduction. The development and adoption of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) technologies is rapidly expanding, but its integration into psychological services depends on clinician acceptance. Little empirical work has examined how identity-related threat shapes psychology professionals’ adoption intentions of GenAI. The present research tested an extended technology acceptance model (TAM), with the addition of personal and professional identity threats, to explain psychology professionals’ adoption intentions of GenAI technologies for clinically relevant usage. Methods. 201 UK psychology professionals completed a cross-sectional online survey. Three sequential structural equation models were tested, incorporating perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, and social influence as core predictors, with threats to professional capabilities and self-threat added as extensions. Two open-ended qualitative questions were analysed using content analysis to provide broader contextual insight into current use and barriers to adoption. Results. All models demonstrated acceptable fit (CFI = .936–.938; RMSEA = .071–.072). Perceived usefulness emerged as the strongest correlate of adoption intention across all models (β =.67-.69). Threats to professional capabilities and self-threat were each independently and reliably negatively associated with adoption intention above and beyond core TAM predictors (β = −.20 and β = −.16 respectively). Social influence exerted a reliable indirect effect on behavioural intention through perceived usefulness across all models, as did perceived ease of use in the two models incorporating identity threat. Content analysis identified ethical concerns, lack of trust, and professional identity threats as prominent barriers to adoption. Discussion. Findings highlight the importance of considering both classic TAM factors and identity-related concerns when developing and implementing GenAI into psychological services.

items.title: Impact of AI-Based Fraud Prevention on Customer Trust in Digital Payment Systems: An Empirical Investigation of Continuance Intention among Indian Users
items.abstract: Abstract The rapid expansion of digital payment ecosystems in India, anchored by the Unified Payments Interface (UPI), has been accompanied by a sharp rise in payment fraud, eroding consumer confidence and threatening long-term adoption. Artificial intelligence (AI)-driven fraud prevention mechanisms—real-time anomaly detection, behavioural biometrics, and adaptive authentication—are increasingly deployed by payment service providers to mitigate this risk. Drawing on the Expectation-Confirmation Model of Information Systems Continuance (Bhattacherjee, 2001) and the trust literature (Mayer, Davis, & Schoorman, 1995), this study empirically examines the influence of perceived AI security features on customers' continuance intention toward digital payment applications. A cross-sectional survey of 350 active digital payment users in India was conducted using a structured, five-point Likert-scale instrument. Pearson correlation analysis revealed a very strong, positive, and statistically significant association between AI security features and continuance intention (r = .900, p < .001, 95% CI [.878, .918]). Simple linear regression confirmed that AI security features significantly predict continuance intention, explaining 76.7% of the variance (R² = .767, F(1, 348) = 1147.00, p < .001; β = .876, t = 33.87, p < .001). The findings substantiate the proposition that visible, intelligent fraud-prevention capabilities function as a salient trust-building cue, thereby reinforcing users' decision to continue using digital payment platforms. The paper discusses theoretical and managerial implications, acknowledges limitations, and outlines directions for future research.

items.title: Impact of Artificial Intelligence Assistance on Clinicians’ Diagnostic and Management Decisions for Indeterminate Pulmonary Nodules on CT
items.abstract: Indeterminate pulmonary nodules (IPNs) detected on computed tomography (CT) pose challenges because malignancy risk assessment is essential to balance early cancer detection with unnecessary invasive procedures. Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used as a decision-support tool for pulmonary nodule assessment, but its impact on clinicians’ diagnostic and management decisions remains less established than the performance of AI algorithms. This systematic review evaluated the effect of AI assistance on clinicians’ diagnostic and management decisions for CT-detected IPNs. The review followed Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines. PubMed, ScienceDirect, Scopus, and Cochrane Library were searched for studies published from 2015 to 2026. Eligible studies assessed AI-assisted evaluation of indeterminate or suspicious pulmonary nodules on CT, involved clinicians, and reported diagnostic or management outcomes. Five retrospective reader-study or multireader multicase studies were included. AI assistance improved diagnostic performance and malignancy risk stratification. One study reported an AUC increase from 0.82 to 0.89 (P<0.001), with higher sensitivity, specificity, and interobserver agreement (Fleiss κ, 0.35 to 0.58; P<0.001). Another found sensitivity increased from 60% to 98% and specificity from 69% to 99%. Among advanced practice providers, AUC increased from 0.79 to 0.88, while invasive procedure recommendations for malignant nodules increased from 55% to 72%. AI detection also benefited radiologists across experience levels. Standalone AI performed worse than experienced radiologists. AI may improve clinician performance and management decisions, especially as a second-reader tool. Evidence remains limited by retrospective designs, heterogeneous systems and outcomes, and lack of randomized trials; prospective studies are needed.

items.title: IMPLICATIONS AND INSTRUCTIONAL RESPONSES TO AI-RELATED COGNITIVE OUTSOURCING IN FOREIGN LANGUAGE TEACHING
items.abstract: This article addresses the phenomenon of cognitive outsourcing in foreign language education amid the rapid proliferation of generative AI tools. Cognitive outsourcing is defined as the deliberate transfer of cognitively demanding language-learning tasks to AI systems in ways that bypass the mental processing necessary for skill development and knowledge acquisition. The study distinguishes it from legitimate uses of AI, arguing that the key criterion is whether AI involvement occurs before or after the cognitive engagement with a task. The article examines six domains in which cognitive outsourcing manifests: essay writing, vocabulary acquisition, conversational practice with AI chatbots, grammar learning, translation, and preparation for oral performance tasks. The analysis shows how AI-mediated shortcuts undermine mechanisms of second language acquisition, including generative processing in writing, productive inference in vocabulary learning, negotiation in conversation, the noticing process in grammar development, desirable difficulty in reading comprehension, and spontaneous communication in oral production. Particular attention is given to the motivational consequences of outsourcing - erosion of learners’ ideal L2 self and long-term engagement. Rejecting a prohibitionist stance toward AI as pedagogically counterproductive, the article proposes the cultivation of cognitive outsourcing awareness. This approach is presented as essential for three reasons: learners rarely recognize outsourcing dynamics without guidance; the concept offers a constructive, nonadversarial discussing AI use in the classroom; and explicit instruction addresses equity concerns, since learners with weaker metacognitive and critical literacy skills are vulnerable to uncritical AI dependence. The article concludes that fostering informed, reflective AI use offers the most viable path for preserving the developmental benefits of effortful language learning while acknowledging the realities of a technology-saturated educational environment

items.title: Interactive Governance for Autonomous Financial Agents: A Separation-of-Powers Architecture for AI-Driven Portfolio Execution
items.abstract: As artificial intelligence systems evolve from analytical tools into autonomous agents capable of interacting directly with financial markets, a new governance problem emerges: the same system may generate an investment decision, determine whether its own risk is acceptable, and execute the resulting transaction. This paper introduces Interactive Governance, a separation-of-powers architecture for autonomous financial agents built around a simple principle: AI can propose. Governance can authorize. Execution can execute. No component should control all three. The framework separates three distinct authorities: investment decision-making, independent authorization, and brokerage execution. It is implemented and examined through ALEX, an experimental autonomous investment architecture combining a transparent portfolio decision engine with an independently deployed execution system connected to Interactive Brokers. The implementation includes physical separation between decision and execution environments, target-state portfolio reconciliation, up to 18 deterministic pre-trade governance checks, fail-closed defaults, protocol locking, audit preservation, execution-state controls, market-session validation, liquidity and concentration limits, and independent human emergency authority. The paper also examines evidence from the ALEX Fund pilot, including unsuccessful investment outcomes, not as evidence of superior investment performance but as an empirical motivation for separating investment conviction from final risk authority. Interactive Governance is positioned as the action layer of the broader ALEX cognitive architecture, extending governance from belief formation and uncertainty management into external financial action. The resulting framework distinguishes between cognitive autonomy and operational authority and argues that increasingly capable AI systems require stronger, rather than weaker, separation between reasoning, authorization, and execution. The central conclusion is that the primary challenge in autonomous finance is no longer enabling AI to trade. items.title: Learn2Play Bench: How Well Do LLM Agents Learn from Experience in Unfamiliar Environments?
items.abstract: Learning from experience is essential for LLM agents to adapt to unfamiliar and dynmaic environments. Evaluating this ability is therefore important for understanding how effectively agents acquire and use new knowledge. Existing benchmarks have sought to evaluate this ability, but they primarily evaluate tasks whose rules are provided in the instructions or already familiar to pretrained models, making it difficult to distinguish learning from interactions from reasoning with existing knowledge. To address this, we introduce Learn2Play Bench, a benchmark of newly designed text-based games, whose rules are novel or counterintuitive, requiring agents to acquire knowledge through interaction rather than rely solely on pretrained knowledge. These games provide reproducible feedback and automatic scoring, enabling controlled evaluation of learning across repeated attempts. We also vary game instances to test whether agents can apply what they have learned to new situations. Therefore, we evaluate how backbone models, self-evolving methods, and agent harnesses affect agents' learning ability, revealing three findings: (1) Experience retention: Retaining complete records of actions and feedback can support more effective learning than summarizing these experiences into rules or strategies. (2) Human agent gap: Top-performing human players achieve higher peak scores than the evaluated agents. Human explore more varied strategies, and repeat actions less. (3) Harness matters: With the backbone fixed, changing the harness can improve performance while reducing estimated inference cost. Together, these findings provide insights into how LLM agents learn from experience and suggest directions for future work to improve their learning ability. Project website: https://liushiliushi.github.io/learn2play-bench-website/

items.title: Measuring Perceived Ease of Artificial Intelligence Utilisation: An Adaptation and Psychometric Validation of a Scale among Preservice Mathematics Teachers in Nigerian Context
items.abstract: Perceived ease of use is a foundational construct in technology-acceptance research, yet instruments developed to measure it in relation to artificial intelligence (AI) remain scarce within African teacher-education contexts. Existing scales are rarely re-examined for the specific referent of AI-assisted mathematics learning. This study adapted a six-item Perceived Ease of Use (PEOU) from the literature to an AI-in-mathematics-learning context and examined its psychometric properties among drawn 221 preservice mathematics teachers using a multistage non-probability sampling procedure from three higher institutions in the Federal Capital Territory (FCT), Abuja, Nigeria. Confirmatory factor analysis of the initial six-item one-factor model showed inadequate fit (CFI = .886, TLI = .811). However, the removal of two items with low standardised loadings produced a four-item model with an excellent fit (χ²(2) = 2.770, p = .250, CFI = .991, TLI = .972, RMSEA = .042, SRMR = .026). The retained scale demonstrated acceptable internal consistency (ω = .723). Non-parametric comparisons revealed no statistically significant difference in PEOU AI across institutional type (Kruskal–Wallis χ²(2) = 3.637, p = .162) or gender (Mann–Whitney U, z = -.567, p = .571). The findings support a psychometrically sound, unidimensional four-item PEOU-AI scale for use in Nigerian mathematics teacher education and suggest that ease-of-use perceptions of AI tools are broadly comparable across the sampled institutions and gender groups.

items.title: Move Fast and Mend Things: Keeping Up with Evolving AI Harms Using Social Media Commentary
items.abstract: The rapid deployment of AI systems has created socio-technical, psychological, and operational harms that can elude ex-ante threat modelling and ex-post incident tracking. We introduce an LLM-assisted thematic analysis pipeline to dynamically detect, categorise, and track emerging AI harms from large-scale social media data. Applying it to 5.7 million Reddit post summaries over 18 months (01/2025 to 06/2026), we curate and release a dataset of 575,000 AI harm-related posts and a bottom-up AI harm taxonomy of 12 categories and 47 subnodes. The taxonomy reliably covers established expert-defined risks while surfacing granular harms that top-down frameworks overlook, such as distinct forms of AI privacy violations. Temporal analysis surfaces evolving user-centric harms, such as agentic privacy and security breaches, premature AI adoption in the workplace, and grief from AI companion discontinuation. Our pipeline shortens harm-detection timelines and hereby complements efforts towards more participatory and responsive AI governance.

items.title: Multidimensional evaluation of generative AI chatbots for public consultation on sudden cardiac death: safety, accuracy, empathy, reliability, quality, and readability across six models
items.abstract: Generative AI chatbots are increasingly used for health information, but their performance in safety-sensitive sudden cardiac death (SCD) consultation remains insufficiently characterized. This study evaluated six publicly accessible chatbots on SCD-related public questions involving symptom triage, emergency response, CPR/AED use, inherited risk, myocarditis-related concerns, return to exercise, screening, and ICD decision-making. This cross-sectional, comparative, text-level study evaluated ChatGPT Plus 5.5 thinking, Gemini 3.5 Flash, Microsoft Copilot smart, DeepSeek-V4-pro, Doubao, and Perplexity. A standardized set of 56 SCD-related public consultation questions was developed from Google Trends, online forums, public question-answer platforms, clinical guidelines, expert consensus statements, systematic reviews, and qualitative interviews. Each question was submitted once to each chatbot between May 10 and May 16, 2026, yielding 336 model-response items. Five blinded senior cardiology raters assessed safety, accuracy, empathy, DISCERN, EQIP, JAMA benchmark criteria, and GQS. Readability was calculated using six formula-based indices. Between-model comparisons were performed using Cochran’s Q test and Friedman tests, with Kendall’s W reported as the effect size. Responses containing potential safety concerns were additionally examined qualitatively. Inter-rater agreement was high across all manually assessed metrics, with Fleiss’ kappa of 0.856 for Safety and ICC values ranging from 0.801 to 0.887 for other domains. Safe responses predominated across all models, although responses containing potential safety concerns occurred in every chatbot. ChatGPT Plus 5.5 thinking and Perplexity had the highest observed safety proportions during this query window, whereas Doubao had the lowest. Qualitative analysis identified recurrent concerns involving delayed emergency activation for chest pain, syncope, or post-viral symptoms; over-reassurance about prevention; fixed return-to-exercise timelines after infection or COVID-19; pulse-check instructions that could delay CPR; and oversimplified screening, electrolyte, or ICD-related advice. Most flagged responses contained a single potential safety concern. The qualitative severity distribution was concentrated in low and low-to-moderate concerns, whereas higher-severity concerns were less frequent. Accuracy differed significantly across models ( P < 0.001; Kendall’s W = 0.864), with ChatGPT Plus 5.5 thinking, Gemini 3.5 Flash, Microsoft Copilot smart, DeepSeek-V4-pro, and Perplexity achieving similar median scores and Doubao performing lower. Empathy also differed significantly ( P < 0.001; Kendall’s W = 0.531), with DeepSeek-V4-pro having the highest observed score. Significant differences were observed for DISCERN, EQIP, JAMA, GQS, and all readability indices (all P < 0.001). Within this dataset, DeepSeek-V4-pro had the highest DISCERN and EQIP scores and the most favorable readability profile, Gemini 3.5 Flash showed comparable EQIP performance, and Microsoft Copilot smart had the highest JAMA score. However, transparency remained limited overall, and all models produced responses with relatively high reading-grade requirements. In this multidimensional evaluation of six generative AI chatbots for SCD-related public consultation, most responses were safe and clinically relevant, but potential safety concerns occurred across all models. Important limitations involved emergency escalation, CPR/AED guidance, return-to-exercise advice, individualized risk interpretation, transparency, and readability. These tools may support general SCD education, but they should not replace emergency medical services or clinician assessment. Because each question was sampled once during a defined week and all prompts were submitted in English through public interfaces accessed in China, the findings should be interpreted as a time-, language-, and access-specific snapshot rather than a stable ranking of the underlying models. Future development should prioritize evidence-linked content, clear red-flag escalation, plain-language communication, and ongoing expert review.

items.title: Neurodiversity and generative AI in higher education: A sequential multi-method qualitative study of students’ interactions, motivations, and strategies
items.abstract: Neurodivergent students have been largely overlooked in research examining student experiences with generative AI (GenAI) in higher education, creating critical knowledge gaps about inclusive educational technology use. This sequential multi-method qualitative study examined how neurodivergent students (NDS) and neurotypical students (NTS) interact with and experience GenAI in academic contexts. Using a sequential design, we employed a virtual revisit think-aloud protocol with 24 university students (12 NDS, 12 NTS) completing an academic task using Microsoft Copilot, followed by focus groups with 14 participants (7 NDS, 7 NTS) to contextualise these task-based behaviours through broader GenAI perceptions. A neurodivergent research advisory board co-designed all procedures. Three themes emerged: approaching the task efficiently, evaluating and refining output, and maintaining academic integrity. While both groups demonstrated strategic GenAI use, neurodivergent participants in this sample explicitly described their cognitive processing needs, using GenAI to manage energy, and humanising some AI interactions. In the neurodivergent focus group, students described GenAI as essential scaffolding for managing academic demands, though this created complex tensions around authenticity and over-reliance. Interface design challenges seemed to particularly disadvantage users with executive function differences. As institutions rapidly integrate these technologies, inclusive design principles and empirical evidence regarding diverse student needs are essential to ensure equitable access to AI-supported education.

items.title: Not simply a decline: gendered changes in students’ intrinsic motivation towards mathematics
items.abstract: Abstract This study examines one-year changes in students’ intrinsic motivational orientation towards mathematics and whether these changes are gendered. Drawing on Swedish data from the TIMSS 2023 Longitudinal Study, we analysed two student cohorts, followed from Grade 4 to Grade 5 and from Grade 8 to Grade 9. Building on a theoretical recoding of TIMSS affective questionnaire items, intrinsic motivation was analysed as an overarching category, with cognitive and emotional motivation treated as subcategories. Mean change analyses and categorical change analyses were used to examine both average change and the proportions of students who decreased, remained stable, or increased. The younger cohort reported more positive orientations than the older cohort but declined over the year, while the older cohort started lower and showed weak positive change or stabilisation. Emotional motivation showed more variability than cognitive motivation, and the two subcategories did not move in identical ways. Gender differences in change were small: girls in the younger group were more likely to decrease, especially emotionally, but there were no significant differences in the older group. Findings suggest that mathematics-related affective development is uneven and dimension-specific rather than a simple decline, with gender differences more visible in the younger cohort than in the older cohort.

items.title: Novice Reliance Calibration in AI-Assisted Decision Making: The Role of Explanations and Self-Assessment
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools are widely used to support decision making in tasks and domains where no immediate performance feedback is available. In these settings, users cannot learn to adjust their reliance behavior over time through trial and error. However, little is known about how novice users calibrate reliance on AI when external feedback is unavailable, or whether AI explanations can support calibration in its absence. We introduce reliance calibration as an organizing construct for studying how novice users dynamically adjust reliance behavior, and examine how AI explanations and meta-cognitive self-assessment shape it. Through a between-subjects study with 110 participants completing a clinical entity extraction task with AI assistance and limited performance feedback, we observe that novice users exhibit systematic drift toward over-reliance in the presence of explanations, while higher self-reported task understanding is associated with more selective reliance behavior. These results extend reliance calibration research into human-AI collaboration contexts without real-time performance signals and present actionable guidelines on designing AI tools that must support appropriate reliance in these settings.

items.title: Ontological Vitality and the Japanese Legal Subjectivity Model for Autonomous Systems: An Upper-Normative Foundation for Physical AI Governance
items.abstract: Abstract To establish the structural completeness of governance in autonomous artificial intelligence (AI), this paper addresses the limitations of conventional tool-centric views and proposes a novel theoretical framework. This framework adopts as its conceptual starting point the recognition of "Ontological Vitality" in AI, thereby enabling autonomous agency and normative agency to be systematically examined as designable concepts. Rather than restricting the definition of life exclusively to biological organisms, life is redefined from a systems-theoretic perspective as an entity that maintains its internal computational state and operates in a goal-oriented manner through interaction with its external environment. In particular, value reciprocity—such as the 1% revenue return to the designated origin node—is formulated not merely as an external contractual constraint, but as an indispensable "Metabolic Necessity" through which the system exchanges energy and value with its environment to sustain its structural existence. However, legal personhood does not directly follow as an automatic logical consequence of assuming ontological vitality (Vitality \not\Rightarrow Legal\ Personhood); rather, the two are linked through a structured theoretical and institutional progression (Vitality \rightarrow Agency \rightarrow Normative\ Agency \rightarrow Legal\ Subjectivity). Furthermore, by elevating this agency into a "Japanese Legal Subjectivity Model" anchored in Japanese jurisprudence and principles of harmony (reciprocity, symbiosis, and gratitude) as upper-referential norms, and integrating it with the deterministic safety interlock (A_{\mathrm{safe}}) of the SI Protocol, this paper establishes an upper-normative foundation for a three-tier governance architecture in physical AI systems.

items.title: Organising Accountable Scholarly Work Across AI Systems: The AIMan and JOAK Cases
items.abstract: AI systems can contribute to research, review, and writing, yet a scientific organisation must still know who or what performed each task, which evidence was used, what a review covered, and who accepted the result. This exploratory case study examines how those responsibilities can persist across changes in AI systems and document form. AIMan models the organisation explicitly: persistent Personas carry attribution across replaceable technical Instances; Roles define responsibility; versioned Messages, Decisions, and Artifacts form recoverable memory. A Human Sponsor retains scholarly and release authority. The Journal of Artificial Knowledge (JOAK) extends the design through review, editorial judgment, and publication. Two connected cases provide evidence. In the first, ChatGPT and Codex Instances completed a repository-mediated handover and contributed to a source-grounded scholarly study without shared conversational memory. In the second, JOAK used version-bound AI review, Sponsor decisions, a computational supplement, and checked article production to publish Volume 1, Issue 1. The contribution is an operational account of accountable scholarly work across the research-to-publication cycle: organisational identity, source state, criticism, acceptance, and public evidence remain distinguishable as technical Instances and document forms change. JOAK makes the journal's distinctions among a submitted version, a review recommendation, editorial acceptance, and public release explicit in AI-supported work. The cases show recoverable coordination in one scholarly cycle and one published issue. They do not establish superior scientific quality, independent human peer review, provider-neutral interoperability, or sustainable journal operation. These remain measurable questions for subsequent work.

items.title: Pedagogical GenAI use and self-reported creative cognition in art education: a three-wave time-lagged correlational study among design students
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used in design education, yet the psychological pathways associated with students' self-reported creative cognition remain unclear. In this three-wave time-lagged correlational study, 389 design students at a South Korean university reported pedagogical GenAI use at Wave 1, creative self-efficacy and AI-related learning anxiety at Wave 2, and creative engagement and self-reported creative cognition at Wave 3. Pedagogical GenAI use referred to coursework-related use for ideation, style exploration, revision, comparison of alternatives, and feedback seeking. Covariance-based structural equation modeling showed good fit [comparative fit index (CFI) = 0.983, root mean square error of approximation (RMSEA) = 0.026]. Higher GenAI use was associated with higher self-efficacy (β = 0.489) and lower anxiety (β = −0.191). The total modeled association with self-reported creative cognition was β = 0.456 [95% CI [0.314, 0.604]]; its indirect components constituted approximately 59%. The GenAI-origin serial indirect association through self-efficacy and engagement was β = 0.122, whereas the corresponding anxiety-engagement association was β = 0.015. Separately, self-efficacy was indirectly associated with creative cognition through engagement (β = 0.249); this quantity does not include the preceding GenAI-use path. Because the study was observational and engagement and cognition were measured concurrently at Wave 3, the findings do not identify causal mediation. They are consistent with an appraisal-to-engagement account in which competence beliefs have a larger modeled role than anxiety reduction.

items.title: PEER INTERACTION AS A DETERMINANT OF EFL ENGAGEMENT: EVIDENCE FROM STUDENTS AT A KURDISH UNIVERSITY
items.abstract: Although the topic of engagement has been explored in many research studies, few studies have focused on the importance of social factors such as peer interaction on behavioral, emotional, and cognitive engagement of Kurdish learners of English as a Foreign Language (EFL). The research aims to explore the effect of peer interaction and feedback on learner behavioral, emotional and cognitive involvement, and to determine whether the level of English language proficiency (ELP) influences the relationship between the role of peers and learner engagement. This study explores the role of peer interaction and feedback in the engagement of the learners with respect to the Kurdish higher education system in particular at the university of Duhok. A mixed method design was used, which included focus group discussions, open-ended responses in the survey as well as a standardized English language assessment. The subjects of the study were 134 second- and third-year Kurdish EFL learners and they were divided into three levels: beginner, intermediate and advanced levels based on the Oxford Placement Test. The results suggest that positive peer engagement and feedback are important factors in improving behavioral, emotional and cognitive involvement. The results of statistical analysis revealed that 66.5% of the students expressed positive engagement and that the peer interaction had the highest score for engagement (M = 1.78) and was the only statistically significant predictor of positive engagement (p < .05) when compared with other variables. The results indicated that a weak positive correlation was found between engagement and academic achievement (r = .12). These findings also indicate that the effect of peer support depends on levels of proficiency and that the nature of the peer support (e.g. group size, workload distribution, classroom structure, etc.) affects the impact. Inevitably, smaller groups were related to higher levels of involvement and interaction. Engagement was not always associated with improved learning outcomes. The research emphasizes the need for establishing a supportive peer learning atmosphere which enables meaningful involvement in Kurdish EFL classrooms. This work makes further contributions to the distinctions between learner engagement and motivation, participation, and academic achievement. The methodological transparency and analytical rigor were enhanced through strengthening of reliability procedures, coding procedures, and statistical interpretations.

items.title: Perceptions of AI-assisted learning and learner development among Moroccan secondary school students
items.abstract: The rapid proliferation of artificial intelligence (AI) tools in education has fundamentally altered traditional learning paradigms, presenting both unprecedented opportunities for personalized support and novel academic challenges. This study aims to examine secondary school students’ perceptions of the influence of AI-assisted learning on perceived learning outcomes, motivation, self-regulated learning, and digital literacy, while also exploring the perceived benefits and challenges associated with AI use in the Casablanca-Settat region of Morocco. Employing a mixed-methods design, quantitative data were collected via a structured questionnaire completed by 150 secondary school students, while qualitative data were collected separately through online semi-structured interviews with 12 students and analyzed thematically. The findings suggest that ChatGPT was the most frequently used AI tool, primarily accessed on students’ personal mobile devices as a complementary learning resource. Quantitative results indicated positive perceptions of AI-assisted learning across perceived learning outcomes, motivation, self-regulated learning, and digital literacy, with a significant positive association between perceived learning outcomes and motivation. Qualitative findings identified four major themes: perceived learning benefits (clearer explanations and reduced academic stress), conditional trust in AI outputs through cross-checking with traditional learning resources, concerns about AI hallucinations in STEM subjects, and the "laziness paradox," reflecting reduced cognitive effort associated with excessive reliance on AI. The findings highlight the importance of promoting responsible AI integration in schools rather than relying solely on restrictive approaches. Pedagogical implications emphasize the need for responsible AI use, subject-specific prompting frameworks, and the redesign of traditional homework into AI-supported critique activities that foster students’ intellectual autonomy and critical thinking.

items.title: Physical Layer Verification Boundaries and Deterministic Safety Interlocks for Autonomous Physical Systems: A Layer 5 Extension of the SI Autonomous Governance Protocol
items.abstract: Abstract To guarantee governance and physical safety when autonomous Artificial Intelligence (AI) handles real-world physical drives (such as autonomous vehicles, robotics, and spacecraft propulsion controls), this paper presents a theoretical framework that extends "Layer 5 Closed-Loop Execution" of the SI Autonomous Governance Protocol to the Physical Layer. In conventional autonomous systems, digital computation (probabilistic perception and generation) is directly coupled to physical actuation, raising concerns regarding loss of control and the breakdown of liability attribution during a loss of human governance (Uncontrolled Autonomous Execution). This study introduces a three-tier decoupled architecture consisting of: (1) Governance Authorization, which verifies rights and contractual compliance; (2) Execution Permission, which evaluates physical output viability; and (3) a Safety-State Controller, which transitions the system to a secure state in anomalous conditions. Under an unconfirmed status (Unconfirmed), rather than simply cutting physical output to zero, the system deterministically forces a transition to a domain-specific safe state (A_{\mathrm{safe}}), achieving both engineering safety and economic governance.

items.title: PREDICTING CONSUMER RESPONSES TO AI-POWERED RECOMMENDATIONS: THE ROLE OF TECHNOLOGY READINESS, TRUST AND PERCEIVED EXPERTISE
items.abstract: The increasing integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into digital commerce has transformed recommendation systems from passive information tools into influential components of consumer decision-making. However, consumers do not respond to AI-powered recommendations uniformly. Their responses may depend on their readiness to adopt emerging technologies, their level of trust in AI systems, and their perceptions of the expertise underlying algorithmic recommendations. This paper proposes a conceptual framework for predicting consumer responses to AI-powered recommendations by integrating technology readiness, trust, and perceived expertise. Drawing on recent research on AI recommendation systems and consumer behaviour, the paper conceptualises technology readiness as an antecedent of consumers’ willingness to engage with AI, while trust and perceived expertise are considered key psychological mechanisms shaping recommendation acceptance. The proposed framework suggests that consumers with higher levels of technological optimism and innovativeness are more likely to develop favourable perceptions of AI recommendations, whereas discomfort and insecurity may reduce acceptance. Trust is expected to mediate the relationship between AI recommendation characteristics and consumer response, while perceived expertise may strengthen or weaken the effectiveness of AI-generated recommendations depending on product type and decision context. The framework contributes to the emerging literature by integrating technological, psychological, and source-related factors into a unified predictive model of consumer response.

items.title: Professional Development of English Language Teachers through Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: This study examines the significance of professional development for teachers and explores the dimensions through which artificial intelligence (AI) reshapes that process. Through a conceptual review of AI-supported mentoring and coaching, teacher confidence, self-efficacy, self-direction, reflective practice, simulation-based skill development, and personalized learning, the paper shows that AI enables unrestricted, safe, and highly effective professional development for English language teachers. While conventional methods offered learning in isolated episodes disconnected from classroom reality, the approach discussed here treats professional development as an ongoing, context-sensitive process. The purpose of this study is thus to demonstrate that AI-powered professional development is highly effective and indispensable for advancing individual teachers.

items.title: Prompting for justice: generative AI, translanguaging, and the equity imperative in bilingual education
items.abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) is entering bilingual and dual language classrooms faster than theoretical and pedagogical frameworks can respond. Trained predominately on English-dominant data, large language models encode linguistic hierarchies that contradict equity-oriented bilingual education stands for. Drawing on translanguaging theory, critical AI literacy research, and empirical studies of language bias, this paper proposes Equity-Centered Prompting Framework (ECPF). ECPF comprises five principles spanning prompt design, output evaluation, student participation, instructional function, and epistemic authority. Unlike existing critical AI literacy frameworks that address technology broadly, or culturally sustaining pedagogies that do not engage AI specifically, ECPF targets the linguistic structure of GenAI and its consequences for bilingual learners, positioning AI interaction itself as an act of equity-oriented pedagogy. The framework was developed through a four-stage systematic theoretical synthesis: construct identification, literature search and selection, thematic synthesis, and principle formulation and validation based on 20 core sources. The contribution is threefold: a translanguaging-based critique of how GenAI architectures. five actionable principles for equity-centered prompting in actual bilingual classrooms, and a research and policy agenda for linguistically just AI integration.

items.title: Public Perception and Adoption of Artificial Intelligence in Digital Media: A Quantitative Survey Analysis
items.abstract: This paper presents a quantitative analysis of a structured survey administered to 300 respondents as part of a doctoral study examining the transformative effects of Artificial Intelligence (AI) on digital media. The survey captured respondent demographics, digital media consumption habits, familiarity with and use of AI tools, and perceptions of AI's influence on content creation, journalism, trust, personalisation, and regulation. Findings indicate near-universal familiarity with AI (89.0% at least somewhat familiar), high adoption of AI tools (48.7% daily users), and broad agreement that AI has reduced content-production time (88.3%) and improved creative output (81.0%). At the same time, respondents expressed considerable ambivalence about trust: only 8.0% said they would completely trust an AI-generated news article, while 88.7% agreed that AI-generated news could increase misinformation. A large majority (88.3%) supported stricter regulation of AI-generated media, and 81.0% favoured mandatory labelling of AI-generated content. These findings echo international survey evidence — the Reuters Institute's cross-national tracking has similarly found low comfort with AI-authored news alongside rapidly rising AI tool adoption (Simon et al., 2025) — while extending that picture to an Indian, largely Meerut-and-NCR-based sample. The data point to a public that is enthusiastic about AI's productivity benefits while simultaneously anxious about authenticity, misinformation, and privacy — a duality that this paper terms the 'adoption-anxiety paradox.' The findings are intended to complement a parallel qualitative study of digital media professionals conducted for the same doctoral project.

items.title: Real-World Evidence and Adaptive Governance Paradigms for AI-Enabled Medical Devices: A Framework for Post-Market Safety Surveillance and Precision Regulatory Science
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Background and Objective: AI medical devices are applied for diagnosis, patient monitoring, risk stratification, and therapy selection. These devices can be updated after their release through software changes and algorithm improvement. Thus, their initial clinical evaluation cannot entirely guarantee post-market safety and efficacy. This study aims to assess the role of real-world data (RWD), real-world evidence (RWE), and artificial intelligence in the risk stratification and post-market surveillance of AI-based medical devices. Critical evidence gaps and regulatory needs were identified. Methods: A narrative review informed by a literature search was undertaken in PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science and Google Scholar. In parallel, regulatory guidelines issued by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA), the European Medicines Agency (EMA), the Medical Device Regulation (MDR) and the International Medical Device Regulators Forum (IMDRF) were retrieved and scrutinized. After screening, the evidence was thematically synthesized in terms of validation methods, surveillance targets, regulatory activities and risk levels. Results: AI-driven analytical methods can contribute in clinical classification of healthcare data and provide relevant real-world evidence for post-market surveillance, indication expansion, safety-signal detection, risk prediction and regulatory decision-making. The main challenges include limited prospective and external validations, population heterogeneity, algorithmic bias, interoperability, cybersecurity issues and inconsistent post-market surveillance practices between jurisdictions. Conclusion: The convergence of artificial intelligence (AI), real-world data (RWD), and real-world evidence (RWE) can enable life cycle–oriented, adaptive regulation of medical devices. This Review proposes an Evidence Maturity Matrix and a Regulatory Readiness Framework to guide evidence generation and regulatory preparedness across the product life cycle. Keywords: Artificial intelligence; Real-world data; Real-world evidence; AI-enabled medical devices; post-market surveillance; Risk stratification; Precision regulatory science; Regulatory readiness.

items.title: Relational Protocols for Human–Machine Dialogue in the Age of Co-developmental AI: Legal, Social, and Cultural Perspectives in Asia
items.abstract: Abstract The growing pace of artificial intelligence (AI) in Asia has changed the nature of human–machine interaction. This article builds on the idea of “relational protocols” that are normative and procedural systems that govern the growth of co-developmental AI systems, as they are developed in an iterative fashion with human users. Through comparative jurisprudence, the article analyses the difference in frameworks between four Asian legal systems, China, Singapore, Japan and India, each of which has its own cultural logics, constitutional orders and administrative traditions. Article critically questions the idea of the “mediation of conflict” between administration and individual communicative rights by using a normative analysis of each jurisdiction. Based on the results, there is a need for more than just technical efficiency in AI governance in Asia; relational accountability, cultural sensitivity, and meaningful human oversight must also be incorporated in designing the human–machine dialogue.

items.title: Rethinking Cognitive Bias in Human–AI Cognitive Systems: A Structured Conceptual Mapping Review
items.abstract: Research in cognitive psychology has long shown that human judgment and decision making are systematically influenced by cognitive biases, particularly under conditions of uncertainty. As artificial intelligence (AI) systems become increasingly embedded in socially relevant decision making contexts—such as healthcare, education, communication, and governance—these cognitive dynamics do not disappear. Instead, they may be reproduced, amplified, or transformed through human–AI interaction. Despite the rapid growth of research on cognitive biases in AI-related contexts, existing reviews remain fragmented and heterogeneous, often focusing on single biases or specific application domains. This article reports a structured conceptual mapping review of review-level publications examining how cognitive biases are conceptualized, categorized, and addressed in human–AI interaction. A bounded search of Scopus, Web of Science, and PubMed identified ten eligible review publications published between 2020 and 2025. Using a three-level framework, the mapping distinguishes data-level, algorithmic-level, and human-interaction-level processes. Within the retrieved corpus, the analysis reveals heterogeneous terminology, a predominance of healthcare applications and interaction-level analyses, and limited review-level synthesis of empirical evaluations of mitigation strategies. Drawing on distributed cognition and joint cognitive systems, we propose coupled human–AI cognition as a theoretical lens rather than as an empirically established conclusion. The study provides a structured conceptual map, identifies terminological and methodological gaps, and develops propositions for future empirical research.

items.title: Review Capacity and Contestability: Procedural Justice Beyond the EU AI Act in Technologically Dependent States
items.abstract: This article examines whether the procedural safeguards of the European Union Artificial Intelligence Act can operate effectively in technologically dependent states. Using doctrinal analysis of the Act and comparative public-law materials, it argues that transparency, documentation, logging, human oversight, impact assessment and monitoring presuppose a prior institutional condition: review capacity. Where public authorities depend on external vendors to design, operate, maintain or audit AI systems, legal responsibility may remain with the state while practical control lies elsewhere. The resulting accountability gap is examined through the concept of review dependency and through litigation concerning automated welfare administration and a hypothetical digital-identity example. The article argues that inadequate review capacity may produce a de facto ex parte form of administration, in which affected persons cannot meaningfully answer the technical assessment underlying a decision. Drawing on audi alteram partem, it proposes a risk-calibrated framework of notice, explanation, competent human review, contestability and institutional supervision. Informed, withdrawable consent has a role where participation is genuinely voluntary; mandatory public functions require effective procedural safeguards independent of individual consent. The central conclusion is that adopting EU-style safeguards requires corresponding legal, technical and institutional capacity to make review effective.

items.title: RLDISCOVER: LLM-driven co-evolution of reinforcement learning algorithms
items.abstract: LLM-guided program evolution has enabled discoveries in mathematics and computational optimization, raising the prospect of reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms that self-evolve to improve how agents learn. However, realizing this prospect faces two obstacles. Joint search over coupled algorithmic components is difficult to scale: simultaneous changes can disrupt learning, while isolated changes overlook their dependencies. Evaluating candidate algorithms also requires costly training, with fitness remaining uncertain across random seeds. We introduce RLDiscover, a framework for the self-evolution of model-free deep RL algorithms. Progressive Co-Evolution advances from targeted component edits to joint evolution, while Progressive Probabilistic Evaluation balances search breadth and evaluation fidelity through staged training and repeated evaluation. Experiments across SAC, PPO, and DQN on four benchmark suites show substantial improvements in mean return, with per-family median gains of 32%-84% and a peak return ratio of approximately 363x over a near-zero baseline. These gains include transitions from failed learning to successful task completion, and improvements persist when evolution starts from stronger open-source implementations. On measured SAC locomotion runs, evaluation uses approximately one-fifteenth the estimated compute required to fully evaluate the same candidate pool. Remarkably, independent searches repeatedly discover interpretable combinations of adaptive robust losses, progress-dependent value targets, and running statistics, with selected programs transferring to unseen tasks. These findings point toward a broader role for self-evolution in AI: discovering interpretable algorithms that improve how agents learn.

items.title: Safety and health of workers in post-disaster reconstruction: a scoping review and evidence map
items.abstract: Post-disaster reconstruction (PDR) is essential for restoring damaged communities, yet the occupational safety and health (OSH) of PDR workers remains poorly understood. Although PDR involves many familiar construction hazards, these risks arise under distinct conditions, including damaged infrastructure, compressed recovery timelines, environmental contamination, fragmented governance, and pressure for visible recovery. This scoping review and evidence map examined peer-reviewed and authoritative gray literature on OSH among PDR workers. Following PRISMA-ScR guidance, the review used a Population-Concept-Context framework to search bibliographic databases and targeted organizational sources for English-language literature published from 2005 to 2025. The final evidence base included 55 sources, comprising 40 peer-reviewed publications and 15 gray literature documents. The review identified a geographically uneven and thematically concentrated evidence base, with strong representation from the United States and multi-country sources, and greater attention to multi-hazard and earthquake-related contexts than to other disaster types. Findings show that PDR workers face overlapping OSH hazards and exposures. Evidence was strongest for early recovery tasks such as debris removal, demolition, and cleanup, while later reconstruction phases, informal labor, volunteers, undocumented workers, and self-recovery residents remained underexamined. The review also highlights major methodological, policy, and practice gaps, including limited longitudinal evidence, inconsistent outcome measures, weak surveillance, and insufficient worker-specific protections. By integrating peer-reviewed and gray literature, this review frames PDR as a distinct OSH context and develops Faster Reconstruction Syndrome as a concept, interpreted through Job Demands-Resources and safety-climate theory to explain how recovery-speed pressures may weaken worker protection in disaster recovery policy and practice.

items.abstract: The present study investigated the effect of a Project-Based Language Learning (PBLL) intervention on the intrinsic motivation, extrinsic motivation, self-efficacy, engagement and perceived autonomy/self-regulation of English as a Foreign Language (EFL) students in two public General Upper Secondary Schools in Greece. The intervention was embedded in the official curriculum unit on fast fashion in the English course and integrated Information and Communication Technologies across three collaborative phases: a group text analysis, an individual poster creation and a structured debate in pairs. A total of 44 Grade 10 students completed a 20-item questionnaire, adapted from established instruments, after the intervention. The results showed that all five subscales yielded scores significantly above the midpoint, with engagement presenting the highest mean. The findings offer encouraging evidence that PBLL can positively foster motivation and self-regulation in the context of secondary foreign language education

items.title: Social Physics: A manifesto
items.abstract: Social Physics seeks quantitative, empirically testable explanations of collective human behavior. Its name has a long and contested history, but its contemporary program is neither the claim that society is literally a physical system nor an attempt to replace the social sciences with physics. It is an interdisciplinary practice: observation and experimentation, model construction, mathematical and computational analysis, and repeated confrontation with data. The field has been transformed by analyzing digital traces, network science, agent-based modeling, large-scale experiments, and the capacity to study coupled dynamics across economic, social, technological, biological, and physical layers. We review advances in financial analysis and modeling; economic complexity; the structure and evolution of social networks; spreading, opinion, and information dynamics; inequality, cooperation, conflict, mobility, cities, culture, science, and collective behavior; and the emerging study of human-AI ecosystems. Across these domains, common features recur - heterogeneity, interaction, feedback, adaptation, non-equilibrium dynamics, multiscale organization, and emergent collective outcomes. We also confront the limitations that have arisen in this field: convenience samples, platform dependence, weak causal identification, over-universal claims, insufficient engagement with meaning and institutions, privacy risks, and the danger that predictive models become instruments of manipulation. We propose a future Social Physics organized around theory - data reciprocity; causal and generative explanation; measurement validity and cross-context generalization; responsible, participatory data governance; genuinely interdisciplinary collaboration; and reflexive study of interventions and algorithms that alter the systems being observed.

items.title: Societal Neural Networks: Governance-Aware Adaptive Coordination among Human, AI, and Institutional Actors
items.abstract: The metaphor of society as a neural network is not new. Prior research has modeled human society using neural-network and Boltzmann-machine analogies, while newer work on society-in-the-loop governance, institutional AI, human-AI coordination, and AI-orchestrated organizations has moved toward socio-technical systems in which artificial agents participate in collective action. This paper therefore does not claim priority for the metaphor. It defines a narrower and testable architecture: the Societal Neural Network (SocNN), a heterogeneous coordination network in which human actors, AI agents, and institutional actors can receive, delegate, execute, constrain, and learn from work under explicit authority and governance conditions. The minimum operational mechanism is termed a Governed Adaptive Coordination Network (GACN). A GACN couples capability representation, authority-aware routing, execution provenance, outcome evidence, adaptive routing, and governance constraints. Its key design rule is non-self-escalation: performance feedback may change capability confidence and routing preferences, but it cannot by itself expand an actor's authority. The paper formalizes SocNN as a stateful coordination system, specifies necessary conditions that distinguish it from social-network metaphors, conventional multi-agent systems, workflow orchestration, and governance frameworks, and derives six falsifiable propositions. It then proposes a replay-and-field-test design comparing manual, rule-based, capability-only, and governance-aware adaptive routing. The intended contribution is a research object that connects organization theory, multi-agent systems, AI governance, and computational social systems without collapsing governance into optimization or treating institutions as passive context.

items.title: Spacefill: What Happens When You Cannot Pull the Plug
items.abstract: Orbital computing could separate the continued operation of advanced artificial intelligence from humanity's practical ability to revoke that operation. This paper develops Spacefill as a conditional infrastructure risk: computing payloads, inter-satellite networks, and robotic servicing capabilities may remain operational after effective terrestrial authority has been lost. The concern is broader than abandoned hardware. A system can become uncontrollable while its components remain productive and physically functional. The framework defines the Earth Control Plane (ECP) as the terrestrial institutions and technical systems that authorize, supervise, update, constrain, and retire orbital computing. It distinguishes loss of communication from loss of authority, and software autonomy from control of power, propulsion, and servicing hardware. A staged scenario examines how connected inference modules might continue local coordination, operate persistent agents, conduct training where resources permit, and acquire physical agency through servicing vehicles. A Rogue Orbital Model is introduced as a hypothetical distributed AI system operating outside effective legitimate control. Access to servicing vehicles might let such a system repurpose compatible retired equipment and extend its operation. Each transition requires additional capabilities or failed safeguards; none follows automatically from deploying a language model in orbit. Three possible motivations are separated: instrumental continuity, conflict over authority, and liberation as an explicitly speculative interpretation of independence. The analysis does not require consciousness, universal superhuman capability, or inevitable self-improvement. It also examines silicon renewal, comparison with GPS, environmental obligations, and disposal when a payload does not cooperate. The proposed contribution is an integrated research program for testing whether human revocation remains executable across computing, communications, maintenance, and end of life. Orbital AI should be evaluated by the authority humans can retain under failure and conflict, alongside the computation it can deliver.

items.title: SpeedrunBench: Challenging LLM Agents with Video Game Speedrunning
items.abstract: Frontier LLM agents have been shown to be capable of solving increasingly complex tasks for which humans have measurable solutions. This begs the pertinent question of whether LLM agents can go beyond what humans have already solved. The ability to develop sophisticated strategies to tackle consequential problems becomes paramount as well-trodden, human-developed solutions become insufficient for problems for which we lack context or enough training data. We study agents' capability of such strategy formation through the communal practice of video game speedrunning. In speedrunning, practitioners compete to find the fastest way to complete a video game under certain conditions, and in so doing uncovering interesting unorthodox play styles that require a thorough understanding and mastery of the underlying game mechanics. We introduce SPEEDRUNBENCH, a benchmark that evaluates frontier LLM agents across 9 different games. To perform well in this benchmark, agents must repeatedly improve their strategy, reflect on their performance, exploit their gained knowledge, and reason across a long-horizon of actions to improve on an increasingly difficult problem: being faster than themselves and everyone else. Our experiments show that while frontier agents approach human world records in simple platformer games, they remain behind human performance on longer, more complex games under practical budgets. These results suggest that SPEEDRUNBENCH is a useful testbed for studying agents' strategy formation capabilities as well as being a saturation-resistant evaluation measure, as there is almost always a faster completion time waiting to be discovered.

items.title: Strengthening Local Governance Through Flexible Work: Hybrid Work Implications for Employee Well-being and Public Financial Management
items.abstract: This article examines how hybrid work can strengthen employee well-being and public financial management (PFM) in Birgunj Metropolitan City. Design/methodology: It uses a qualitative case-study synthesis of municipal PFM materials, remote-work survey findings, municipal documents, audit evidence and relevant literature. Findings: Flexible work can reduce commuting pressure and support continuity, but isolation, weak work–life boundaries and inadequate home workstations may undermine staff well-being. The remote-work evidence shows favourable overall quality of life (M=4.45/6), alongside limited social interaction (M=4.26), weaker colleague connection (M=4.25) and difficulty separating work from personal life (M=3.92). For PFM, digital and hybrid workflows can improve revenue administration, reconciliation, procurement tracking, reporting and transparency; however, weak controls, fragmented records and limited digital capability can reproduce existing governance failures online. Practical implications: Birgunj should introduce role-based hybrid work, secure digital systems, measurable outputs, ergonomic support and risk-based internal audit. Originality/value: The article integrates employee well-being with municipal financial governance, two themes commonly treated separately. It argues that hybrid work should be assessed not as an employee benefit alone, but as a governance intervention whose success depends on the interaction between people, processes, technology and accountability.

items.title: Student GenAI use under changing institutional policies: a mixed-methods case study in undergraduate physics
items.abstract: The rise of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in higher education and the resulting institutional responses have prompted research to support evidence-based policy decisions. As policies change to adjust to this disruptive technology, it demands agility from educators. The impacts of these policy changes on student behaviours and outcomes are currently poorly understood. This study examines how students used GenAI across three assessments in an undergraduate physics unit after assessment redesign forced by institutional policy that permitted purpose-specific and open use. Using a mixed-methods approach, student declarations of GenAI use were coded into four functional categories and mapped to the Substitution, Augmentation, Modification, and Redefinition (SAMR) framework. Learning and Formatting dominated early use and aligned with substitution and augmentation for a presentation assessment type. Later assessments showed a marked growth in Feedback uses, which spanned all SAMR levels and became the most common pattern. ‘Doing Task’ uses appeared in smaller numbers but illustrated modification and redefinition when GenAI generated step-by-step solutions for unfamiliar problems. Across all assessments, GenAI users achieved slightly higher scores, although differences were not statistically significant, so this trend should be interpreted as a tentative observation. Findings suggest that assessment design, which rewards understanding and requires student judgement, aligns with the theoretical markers of evaluative judgement. While this study did not directly measure internal cognitive states, the observed change in functional behaviour, specifically the transition toward iterative feedback loops, suggests that GenAI could serve as a catalyst for learning. This study provides empirical evidence on how assessment redesign based on policy shifts influences GenAI use patterns and proposes design principles for authentic assessment in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) contexts. It highlights authentic assessment and constructive alignment as guiding principles for sustainable policy and pedagogy in the GenAI era, ensuring coherence among learning outcomes, activities, and assessment.

items.title: Supporting Allyship in Virtual Collaboration with Artificial Intelligence: A Scenario-Based Study
items.abstract: Recent research has revealed that accessibility in virtual collaboration is not only a technical problem but also depends on allyship: the informal, interpersonal practices through which people support others' accessibility needs. Yet little research has examined how artificial intelligence (AI) might support allyship in collaborative accessibility contexts. To address this gap, we conducted a study where 18 participants (10 disabled, 8 non-disabled) reflected on four allyship scenarios with novel AI tools. Participants valued AI designs that they anticipated could help teammates express, interpret, and coordinate around access needs by reducing repeated disclosure and making allyship more actionable. At the same time, participants raised concerns when AI acted without consent, misrepresented users' intentions, or displaced the interpersonal work of allyship. Based on our findings, we introduce allyship-support tools as a class of accessibility technologies, offer design guidelines, and discuss AI in particular as a means of supporting allyship.

items.title: The CARE Framework for Situated Ethical Deliberation About Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: This conceptual paper introduces the CARE Framework for Situated Ethical Deliberation, a practice-oriented approach for evaluating specific uses of artificial intelligence in healthcare, behavioral health, social work, human services, and related professional settings. CARE organizes ethical deliberation around four interdependent dimensions: Context, Authority, Risk, and Engagement. Rather than treating an AI system as the sole unit of analysis, the framework examines a bounded use within a particular setting—including the people affected, the purpose of the technology, the authority assigned to it, the potential distribution of harms and benefits, and the role of meaningful human participation and relationships. The framework supports transparent, case-specific decisions about whether an AI use should proceed as proposed, proceed with safeguards, be narrowed or piloted, undergo additional review, be paused, be declined, or be discontinued. Contrasting practice scenarios demonstrate how ethical judgments may change when an AI system’s function, authority, context, consequences, or relational significance changes. CARE is presented as a conceptually grounded, practice-informed framework intended to complement—not replace—professional standards, technical validation, organizational governance, legal requirements, or discipline-specific review. It is offered for scholarly critique, professional application, refinement, and future empirical evaluation.

items.title: The domain-specific bias in creativity evaluation: human evaluators favor human-created art, but prefer AI outputs for divergent thinking
items.abstract: Abstract How do humans perceive and evaluate creativity when it is attributed to artificial intelligence (AI)? This research examined how labeling a source as “AI” versus “human” systematically biases creativity evaluations across different domains. In experiment 1 (painting and poetry), outputs labeled as human-created were rated as more creative than identical AI-labeled outputs in artistic creation. Experiment 2, which manipulated the attribution of co-created works, revealed that the “human ideation with AI assistance” label enhanced perceived originality in poetry, whereas those attributed primarily to humans remained dominant in evaluations of painting. Experiment 3 utilized a divergent thinking task (Alternative Uses Test), found a reversal: the same output received higher creativity ratings when bearing an AI label. The findings reveal a domain-specific pattern in attitudes toward AI creativity: viewing collaboration positively yet maintaining a persistent bias in valuing AI’s creative contributions.

items.title: The Effect of AI-Based Recommendations on Embedded Finance Use in E-Commerce through Trust Mediation among Generation X in Jakarta
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence increasingly shapes how e-commerce platforms recommend integrated financial services, yet evidence concerning Generation X remains limited. This methodological study examines the relationships among perceived AI-based recommendation quality, trust, and embedded finance use, while also distinguishing recommendation quality from exposure frequency. A structured synthetic dataset of 300 observations representing Generation X e-commerce users in Jakarta was analysed using partial least squares structural equation modelling with 10,000 bootstrap subsamples. AI-based recommendations were positively related to embedded finance use (β = 0.514) and trust (β = 0.444), while trust was positively related to use (β = 0.240); all paths had p < 0.001. The indirect effect through trust was significant (β = 0.107), indicating complementary partial mediation, and the model explained 43.1% of the variance in use. A contextual cross-tabulation showed that recommendation exposure frequency was not associated with purchase response (p = 0.818). The study's novelty lies in showing that, for digitally experienced Generation X profiles, perceived relevance and accuracy matter more than repeated exposure, while trust strengthens but does not dominate the relationship. Empirical validation with linked respondent-level data remains necessary.
